text: During periods of high ambient temperatures, the efficiency of air-cooled heat exchangers decreases as the temperature rises. The compressors, which are the most energy-intensive equipment in the liquefaction process, require additional power to maintain the necessary pressure and cooling levels under these conditions. 4.2.3 CO VENTING 2 The liquefaction plant will be designed to minimize CO venting and emissions into the atmosphere, 2 aiming to essentially eliminate the need for venting during normal steady-state operation. The only continuous vent anticipated is from the inert removal unit, which contains approximately 0.27% CO 2 emissions per mass weight of LCO produced. As the tankers are dedicated to this service, CO in heel will 2 2 meet export specification, therefore during the loading of LCO , the returning CO vapor, with a maximum 2 2 flow rate of 1250 m³/h from the carrier, will be redirected back to the compression system. Loading activities to the tanker shall be stopped when the liquefaction plant is not in operation. Both the liquefaction plant and the storage units will be equipped with pressure control valves (PCVs) as the primary protection against overpressure, and pressure safety valves (PSVs) as secondary protection. CO vapor will be released to the atmosphere when the pressure in the system exceeds normal operating 2 levels. In an emergency situation, pressure relief will be managed by the PCVs and the PSVs. Based on previous projects it is anticipated that the CO released from the PSVs can be vented directly to the 2 atmosphere through short tailpipes, maintaining high velocities (greater than 100 m/s) to ensure effective dispersion. These protection assumptions would be confirmed during later design phases. A comprehensive vent and relief study will be conducted in the next engineering phase. This will include defining the key venting scenarios, designing the CO vent system, and conducting dispersion analysis to 2 determine the necessary height and location for the vent stack. Similar analyses on other projects have not demonstrated a requirement for a dedicated knockout (KO) drum and vent stack. However, as this has not been the case on all reference projects, a closed CO vent system comprising a vent KO drum and 2 an elevated vent stack, which will safely dispose of discharged CO at a designated safe location, has been 2 included for this phase. 4.2.4 EXPORT The facility features an export system consisting of 2x100% LCO Ship Loading Pumps (one in operation 2 and one as a spare) with a pumping capacity of 1,250m³/h at an estimated head of 10 bar / 100m. These loading pumps transfer liquid CO via the export metering package to the loading arm, while displaced 2 CO vapor from the ship will return to the plant via the vapor return loading arm and the vapor return 2 metering package. A common spare loading arm is also provided. See Figure 4.2. CO vapor displaced during filling of the storage vessels, any evaporated CO from the storage units, and 2 2 excess CO vapor returned from the ship during offloading will be recycled for liquefaction.
